narrative:
The model estimates a 79% chance that you will leave your job, meaning that among employees with a similar profile, roughly eight in ten are expected to depart. Because the promotion decision is tied to retention risk, the organization is reluctant to invest in a promotion when the model signals a strong likelihood of departure.

The strongest signal was your overall work experience of six to ten years, which pushed the prediction toward leaving; this is more experience than the most common one-to-five-year range among employees predicted to stay. The second signal was that you have received other job opportunities while in this role—only about one in four employees predicted to stay reported that—so the model treats your external options as a strong sign of mobility. Third, your one-to-five years in the current organization also added to the leave risk. In other words, the model is not judging your ability; it is flagging a profile where your experience, outside opportunities, and tenure pattern suggest you may move on.

Before revisiting promotion, you and your manager should discuss your career path, the missed promotion you feel you deserved, access to useful training, and ways to increase recognition, support, and engagement. The organization should consider a concrete retention plan and clearer advancement criteria; you should clarify what would make you stay and what opportunities you want.
